catalog_quote: Phonological words in Bru Tri as in other Katuic languages are either mono- or disyllabic. Because a word with two syllables always has an unstressed first syllable and a dominant second syllable, these languages have sometimes been described as “sesqui-syllabic.” ... Word stress is always found on the final (main) syllable. Yes-no questions are often accompanied by rising intonation and use of the clause-final question particle /tə:/. Other interrogatory sentences are marked by stress on the question marker.

new_statements.quote: The prevailing word pattern of Brũ is CVC/CCVC in which CVC represents a non-stressed, non-obligatory pre-syllable and CCVC a stressed, obligatory main syllable. The pre-syllable exhibits a high degree of vowel neutralization with very little vowel contrast, whereas the main syllable demonstrates full contrast between all vowels.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are sesquisyllabic: an optional unstressed pre-syllable (CVC, with neutralized vowel) plus an obligatory stressed main syllable (CCVC). Stress therefore always falls on the main (final) syllable of the word; in monosyllables it is the only syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned. The same paper (p. 205) adds that the first/second register contrast has nothing to do with pitch: register-pairs are said on the same pitch in isolation and in connected speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('word pattern'); based on the Bru of Hướng Hóa district, Quảng Trị province, South Vietnam (the Vân Kiều dialect), i.e. Eastern Bru proper. The Thailand-side statements (Thongkum 1980 p. 222, Miller & Miller 1994 p. 45) give the same rule for Western Bru / So-Bru dialects.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes the Bru of Hướng Hóa district, Quảng Trị province (South Vietnam), i.e. the Vân Kiều dialect of Eastern Bru [bru], east2332.), which Glottolog files as Western Bru (west2397) or So, not east2332; Thongkum explicitly says her variety is not the dialect studied by Miller in Vietnam.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (rule 01 = final) and as the existing Phillips, Miller & Miller 1976 statement (unstressed pre-syllable, stressed main syllable). It adds an explicit, categorical formulation ('always.. final (main) syllable') and the sentence-level note that non-yes/no questions carry stress on the question marker.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic (unstressed pre-syllable + main syllable); word stress always falls on the final, i.e. the main, syllable. The language has two phonation registers and vowel length, not tone (sec. 2.3 heads 'Suprasegmentals (tones, registers, phonation)' but describes only registers). Interrogatives other than yes-no questions are marked by stress on the question marker (a sentence-level statement).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated ('always'). Sec. 2.1 notes the pre-syllable vowel is usually a neutral mid-central vowel and only rarely contrastive (e.g. /kucit/ 'to die' vs /kacit/ 'to kill').
new_statements.identity_note: Miller 2017 sec. 1 says the variety described is the one Ethnologue calls 'Eastern Bru', known as Bru Tri in Laos (Savannakhet) and Bru Vân Kiều in Vietnam (Quảng Trị, Quảng Bình, resettled groups in Đắk Lắk); sec. 2.3 refers to 'the dialect studied by the author' without naming a village. This is the east2332 variety, not the Western Bru of Thailand.
